February 13
Epiphany 6C — The Sixth Sunday of Epiphany
Colors: green
Jer 17:5-10
Psalm 1
1 Cor 15:12-20
Lk 6:17-26
To the Saints at Vanadium Woods,
February 13, 2022
Grace and peace from our Lord Jesus Christ, the son of our Father in Heaven, now and in the resurrection to come.


In today's New Testament lesson (1 Corinthians 15:1-11), St. Paul is responding to another one of the decisive issues in the Church at Corinth. Some time or other, I opined that perhaps when St. Paul got another letter from Corinth, he looked up at whoever he was traveling with and said, "You know what? Just feed me to the lions!"


It is astonishing to me that St. Paul has to reinforce to the Corinthians that the saints will, in fact, rise from the dead. While teaching, the Sadducees challenged Jesus about the resurrection from the dead. Jesus had to remind them the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is not the God of the dead. Apparently, a Christian version of being a Sadducee arose in Corinth. It sounds like some of the folks in the Church at Corinth believed only Jesus rose from the dead - because he's God, I guess - and the rest of us will not.


I've got to tell you, I just don't understand how you can reasonably come to this conclusion and continue to be a Christian. Seriously, if there is no resurrection from the dead, I don't see any reason not just to do whatever you want to do before you die - even if it is at the expense of others. Later on, St. Paul says, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." No heaven, no hell, no worries. Sort of. 


One of the oddities of the world we live in is that even impossibly wrong-headed beliefs have consequences in the real world. We are seeing it played out now on a large scale. Distrust in science, government, the media, each other, etc., has resulted in the largest discord the world has seen since, I am not sure when.


The belief that Jesus rose from the dead is core to Christianity. And it is a belief based on the accounts of eyewitnesses. I confess I have not talked with Jesus face to face, but those who have, I trust what they wrote. As a consequence, I trust what Jesus has said. The role of the resurrection of Jesus and its witnesses is to affirm the things revealed to us in Scripture. The focus of this section in St. Paul's letter to the Corinthians concerns the promise of our own resurrection from the dead.


I have noticed most people who think about such things worry about whether they will go to heaven or not. I don't recall talking with anyone who has been concerned about dying and then not being dead again [[I confess, in rereading this sentence several times in 2024, I have no idea what I meant. Still, for the sake of being honest about these homilies, I am leaving it here. If you figure it out, let me know]]. I have to include myself in that group. From time to time, I have said, "Fr. Paul says, 'no one gets out alive'." And while that is true, it is not true enough. I think I need to add something like, "and no one gets out dead either."


Trusting that no one gets out alive and that no one gets out dead should have an enormous impact on how we live our lives. Here is a question we should ask ourselves before we get out of bed each day: "If I have to come back to this world after I've left it, is it in a condition I want to come back to? If your answer is “no,” there is work to do.


I have this fear of coming back from the dead and hearing Jesus say something like, "This is how you left it, now clean up your mess." This seems fair to me. St. John's Revelation tells us there will be a new heaven and a new earth (Revelation 21:1). What he literally tells us is "I saw a new heaven and new earth." He doesn't tell us if the new heaven and earth will be new from scratch - like the heaven and earth in Genesis - or if the old heaven and old earth are remade the way they are supposed to be. In this regard, I am certain I hold a minority view; even so, it seems a reasonable reading in light of God saying the original creation is good. And good for God is more than good enough for me.


But whether the new heaven and new earth come as another miraculous work of Our Father in heaven or as the joyous labors of His children is above my pay grade. Either way, I am Ok with it - as if that mattered to Our Father. Seriously, though, what could be better than being a child of Our Father and doing the things Our Father asks and requires of us? 


What is better than doing the things of Our Father is not an abstract question. In different words, Jesus asked the same question in the Garden of Gethsemane when he asked His Father to "take the cup from him." Of course, he added, "I'll do whatever you want." What was asked of him was not easy, but as we discovered, the works of God through Jesus turned out well. There is no reason to doubt that anything hard Our Father asks of us will also turn out well. This is the promise of the Resurrection of Jesus. Whether difficult or straightforward, whether in this life or life in our resurrection, the resurrection of Jesus tells us the work we are called to do, here and now or then and there, will turn out well. I would be remiss if I did not add while we may have reason to fear in the moment, we do not have reason to fear in the end.


We are the children of God and have every reason to joyously celebrate the work Our Father asks of us and does through us.


The peace of God, which passes all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in the knowledge and love of God, and of His Son Jesus Christ our Lord; and the blessing of God Almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, be among you, and remain with you always.
